title: Python Data Structures — Deep Dive
summary: A ten-page handwritten handbook on Python's built-in data structures — lists, tuples, sets, dictionaries, hashing, stacks and queues — covering internals, methods, Big-O complexity and how to pick the right structure. Each page packs definitions, comparison tables, code examples, gotchas and interview tips.

chapters.title: Data Structures Overview
points: Definition: a data structure is a way of organizing and storing data in computer memory so we can access, modify and process it efficiently
Why data structures: store data in an organized way; perform operations efficiently; reduce time & space complexity; solve problems in an optimized way
Comparison table row — List `[1,2,3]`: ordered ✓, mutable ✓, duplicates Yes, index access ✓ — store collection of items, allows duplicates
Comparison table row — Tuple `(1,2,3)`: ordered ✓, mutable ✗, duplicates Yes, index access ✓ — fixed collection of items, faster than list
Comparison table row — Set `{1,2,3}`: ordered ✗, mutable ✓, duplicates No (unique), index access ✗ — unique items, fast lookup, no indexing
Comparison table row — Dictionary `{'a':1,'b':2}`: ordered ✓ (insertion order), mutable ✓, keys no duplicates / values yes, no index access (use keys) — key-value pair mapping, very fast lookup
Footnotes: sets are unordered (no concept of index); dicts preserve insertion order since Python 3.7+
Mutable (can be changed): list, set, dict — Immutable (cannot be changed): tuple, str, int, float, bool, frozenset
Memory trick — LIST = Ordered + Mutable + Duplicates `[10,20,30]`
Memory trick — TUPLE = Ordered + Immutable + Duplicates `(10,20,30)`
Memory trick — SET = Unordered + Mutable + Unique `{10,20,30}`
Memory trick — DICT = Key-Value + Ordered + Unique keys `{'a':1,'b':2}`
When to use List: ordered collection you may modify — e.g. items in cart; Tuple: data fixed and should not change — e.g. coordinates (x,y)
When to use Set: unique items & fast membership checking — e.g. unique usernames; Dict: mapping key → value — e.g. user info (id → name)
Interview tip: always choose the right data structure — it improves code readability and efficiency
Key takeaway: Right Data Structure = Efficient Code

chapters.title: Python Lists
points: List is an ordered collection of items; items can be any data type; mutable (can be changed); duplicates allowed
Mixed-type example: `my_list = [10, 'abhi', 3.14, True]`
Indexing on `my_list = [10,20,30,40,50]`: positive index 0..4, negative index -5..-1; `my_list[0]` → 10 (first), `my_list[2]` → 30, `my_list[-1]` → 50 (last)
Method `append(x)` — add item at end: `lst.append(60)` → [10,20,30,60]
Method `extend(iterable)` — add multiple items: `lst.extend([70,80])` → [10,20,30,70,80]
Method `insert(i, x)` — insert x at index i: `lst.insert(1,15)` → [10,15,20,30]
Method `remove(x)` — remove first occurrence: `lst.remove(20)` → [10,30]
Method `pop([i])` — remove & return item at index i, default last: `lst.pop()` → 30, `lst.pop(0)` → 10
Methods `clear()` → [], `index(x)` → index of first occurrence (`lst.index(30)` → 2), `count(x)` → `lst.count(10)` → 2
Methods `sort()` in-place → [10,20,30], `reverse()` in-place → [30,20,10]
Example program: `lst=[5,1,8,3]; lst.append(10); lst.sort(); print(lst) # [1,3,5,8,10]; print(lst[1:4]) # [3,5,8]`
Big-O: access (indexing) O(1); search O(n); insertion at end O(1) amortized; insertion any position O(n); deletion at end O(1); deletion any position O(n)
Interview tip: lists are versatile and used almost everywhere — know the methods well and analyze time complexity for insertions and deletions

chapters.title: List Internals & Complexity
points: Python list is implemented as a dynamic array — it stores references (addresses) to objects in contiguous memory
The array can grow and shrink as needed; when size exceeds current capacity a new larger array is created and elements are copied
Memory picture: `my_list=[10,20,30,40]` occupies slots 0–3 with slots 4–7 None — Used = 4, Capacity = 8
Note: capacity is usually >= size; this extra space is what makes append efficient
Dynamic resizing: when the list runs out of space Python allocates a new array with more capacity
Growth trace: capacity 4/size 4 → append(50) capacity 8/size 5 → append(60) size 6 → append(70) size 7 → append(80) capacity 16/size 8
New capacity is roughly ~2x the old capacity (actually ~1.125x + constant in CPython)
Why append is amortized O(1): most of the time append just drops the item in free space → O(1)
Occasionally resizing happens → O(n) because elements are copied, but these costly operations are rare
Over a large number of appends the average cost per append is O(1)
Amortized analysis: n appends → total cost O(n) ⇒ amortized cost per append = O(1)
Complexity table: access by index O(1); search in unsorted list O(n); append (end) O(1) amortized; pop (end) O(1)
Complexity table: insert at beginning O(n); insert at any position O(n); delete at beginning O(n); delete at any position O(n); slice (copy) O(k) where k = number of elements
Example program using `sys.getsizeof` in a loop over `range(1,21)` to watch capacity grow as items are appended
Important points: list keeps extra space for future growth; `append()` is amortized O(1), not worst-case O(1)

chapters.title: Python Tuples
points: Tuple is an ordered collection of items; immutable (cannot be changed after creation); duplicates allowed; implemented as a fixed-size sequence; more memory efficient than list
Creating tuples: `t1=(1,2,3,4)` parentheses; `t2=1,2,3,4` without parentheses; `t3=tuple([1,2,3])` from list; `t4=()` empty; `t5=(10,)` single element
Gotcha: `(10)` is not a tuple, it is just an integer — `(10,)` with the trailing comma is a one-element tuple
Immutability: once created you cannot change, add or remove elements; any modifying operation raises an error
Error examples on `t=(1,2,3)`: `t[0]=100` → TypeError; `t.append(4)` → AttributeError; `del t[1]` → TypeError
Packing: `t = 10, 20, 30` then `print(t)` → (10,20,30)
Unpacking: `a,b,c = t` then `print(a,b,c)` → 10 20 30
Swapping with tuple unpacking: `x,y = 5,10` then `x,y = y,x` → prints 10 5
Tuple methods: `count(x)` returns count of x (`t.count(10)` → 2); `index(x)` returns first index of x (`t.index(30)` → 2) — only these two
Tuple vs List row — Mutable: No (immutable) vs Yes (mutable); Syntax: ( ) vs [ ]
Tuple vs List row — Memory: Less vs More; Speed: Faster vs Slower
Tuple vs List row — Methods: few (count, index) vs many; Use case: fixed/safe data vs dynamic data
When to use a tuple: data should not change; using it as a dictionary key (lists cannot be keys); returning multiple values from a function; when you want better performance than a list

chapters.title: Python Sets
points: Set is an unordered collection of unique items; duplicates not allowed; elements must be hashable (immutable types); sets themselves are mutable; very fast membership testing
Example: `s={10,20,30,40}`, `type(s)` → <class 'set'>; `s={10,20,20,30,30,40}` removes duplicates automatically; `print(s)` → {40,10,20,30} (order may vary)
Basic operations table: add element `s.add(50)` → {10,20,30,40,50}; add multiple `s.update([5,6])` → {5,6,10,20,30,40}
Basic operations table: `s.remove(30)` removes element; `s.discard(100)` → no error for a missing element; `s.pop()` returns & removes an arbitrary element; `s.clear()` → set(); `len(s)` → 5
Set operations — Union (∪) `A | B` gives all unique elements: A={1,2,3}, B={3,4,5} → {1,2,3,4,5}
Set operations — Intersection (∩) `A & B` gives common elements → {3}
Set operations — Difference `A - B` gives elements in A but not in B → {1,2}
Set operations — Symmetric difference `A ^ B` gives elements not common → {1,2,4,5}
Membership testing on `s={10,20,30,40}`: `20 in s` → True; `999 in s` → False; `100 not in s` → True
Why fast: sets use hashing under the hood, so membership testing is O(1) on average
Unordered nature: `s1={1,2,3,4}`, `s2={4,3,2,1}`, `s1==s2` → True — order does not matter
Tip: do not rely on the order of elements in a set; if order is needed use a list or tuple
Time complexity: add (add/update) O(1); remove (remove/discard) O(1); membership (in/not in) O(1); pop O(1); union/intersection/difference O(n)
When to use a set: you need unique items; fast membership testing; order is not important; mathematical set operations
Important note: elements in a set must be immutable (hashable) — allowed: int, float, str, tuple, frozenset; not allowed: list, dict, set
Interview Q: why are lists not used for membership testing in large datasets? A: list lookup is O(n) while set lookup is O(1) on average

chapters.title: Python Dictionaries
points: Dictionary is an unordered* collection of key-value pairs; keys must be unique and hashable (immutable types); values can be any type and duplicated; dicts are mutable; implemented using a hash table
Example dict with mixed value types: `d = {'name':'Abhi', 'age':23, 'skills':['Python','SQL','Git'], 'is_employed':True}`
Since Python 3.7+ dictionaries preserve insertion order
Internals: the key is passed through a hash function which returns an index; the key-value pair is stored at that index; gives average O(1) for lookup, insert and delete
Hash walkthrough: Key 'age' → hash('age') = 5721 → index 5721 % 8 = 1 → slot 1 of a size-8 hash table holds 'age': 23
Note: collisions can occur; Python handles them using open addressing
Method `get(key, default)` returns value for key, or default when key not found: `d.get('age')`, `d.get('city','NA')`
Methods `keys()` all keys, `values()` all values, `items()` key-value pairs as tuples
Method `update(other_dict)` merges key-value pairs from another dict: `d.update({'age':24})`
Methods `pop(key, default)` removes key and returns its value; `popitem()` removes and returns an arbitrary key-value pair (LIFO in 3.7+); `clear()` removes all items
Methods `copy()` returns a shallow copy; `setdefault(key, val)` returns value of key or inserts key with val if missing: `d.setdefault('city','Pune')`; `len(d)` number of pairs

Basic operations on `d={'a':1,'b':2}`: `d['c']=3` add/update; `d['a']` access → 1; `d['b']=20` update; `del d['a']` delete; `'c' in d` membership → True; `len(d)` → 2; `for k in d: print(k, d[k])` iterates keys
Dictionary comprehension: `squares = {x: x*x for x in range(1,6)}` → {1:1, 2:4, 3:9, 4:16, 5:25}
Time complexity (average case): access `d[key]` O(1); search `key in d` O(1); insert/update O(1); delete `del d[key]` O(1); `len(d)` O(1)
Remember: dictionary gives O(1) average complexity because of hashing; in the worst case (many collisions) it can degrade to O(n)
Interview tip: dictionary is best used when you need fast lookups using keys

chapters.title: Hashing Deep Dive
points: Hashing converts a key into an integer using a hash function; that integer locates the value in a dict or set; enables fast average O(1) lookup, insertion and deletion
A hash function takes an input (key) and produces a fixed-size integer (hash value); the same input always produces the same hash value; Python provides the built-in `hash()`
Hashable objects have a hash value and can be used as dict keys or set elements; unhashable objects cannot be hashed
Hashable: int, float, str, tuple (of hashables) — Unhashable: list, set, dict
`hash([1,2,3])` → TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'
Why lists cannot be dict keys: lists are mutable, so if a list key's contents changed its hash would change, breaking the hash-table contract — Python raises TypeError
`d = {[1,2]: 'value'}` → TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'
Dict and set internals: both are implemented using hash tables; keys (or elements) are hashed to an index
Collision: two different keys produce the same hash value — e.g. 'abc' and 'cab' both hash to 12345 → Index 5
Python handles collisions internally using open addressing with probing / chaining; this is rare and handled efficiently
`hash()` returns the hash of an object, works only on hashable objects, and hash values are integers: `hash('hello')` → -325234333; `hash(42)` → 42; `hash(3.14)` → 322818021
Custom objects: by default user-defined objects are unhashable — define `__hash__()` and `__eq__()` to make them hashable
Example `class Point` with `__init__(self,x,y)`, `__hash__` returning `hash((self.x, self.y))`, and `__eq__` comparing x and y

Summary: hashing converts keys to integers; enables O(1) average lookup; only hashable objects can be dict/set keys; collisions handled internally; understanding hashing is key to mastering dicts and sets

chapters.title: Stacks & Queues
points: Stack stands for Last In First Out (LIFO); elements are added and removed from the same end called TOP; real-life examples: undo operation, browser back button, function call stack
Stack using list: `stack=[]`; `stack.append(10/20/30)` push; `stack.pop()` returns 30; `stack[-1]` peek → 20; `len(stack)` size; `stack.clear()` clear stack
Stack complexity: push (append) O(1); pop() O(1); peek ([-1]) O(1); isEmpty O(1)
Note: in a list `pop(0)` is O(n) because all elements need to be shifted
Queue stands for First In First Out (FIFO); elements are added at the REAR and removed from the FRONT; real-life examples: line at a ticket counter, printing jobs, BFS traversal
Queue using `collections.deque`: `from collections import deque`; `q=deque()`; `q.append(10/20/30)` enqueue; `q.popleft()` returns 10; `q[0]` front → 20; `len(q)` size; `q.clear()`
Deque-as-queue complexity: enqueue (append) O(1); dequeue (popleft) O(1); peek (q[0]) O(1); isEmpty O(1)
Note: using a list for a queue is inefficient because `pop(0)` is O(n)
Queue using list (not recommended): `q=[]`; `q.append(10/20/30)` enqueue; `q.pop(0)` dequeue → O(n)
Why O(n)? when we call `pop(0)` all remaining elements are shifted one position to the left
Common stack uses: undo/redo in editors, backtracking problems, expression evaluation, function call management (recursion)
Common queue uses: CPU task scheduling, printer queue, breadth first search (BFS), handling requests in web servers
Queue operations table: Enqueue → `append(x)` add x at rear; Dequeue → `popleft()` remove and return front; Peek → `q[0]` get front element; isEmpty → `len(q)==0`; Size → `len(q)`
Interview tip: always mention the time complexity while choosing between list and deque
Key takeaway: Stack → LIFO (use list); Queue → FIFO (use deque)

chapters.title: Choosing the Right Data Structure
points: Comparison row — List: mutable Yes, ordered Yes, duplicates Yes, access O(1) by index, search O(n) — use for an ordered collection with frequent changes and duplicates
Comparison row — Tuple: mutable No, ordered Yes, duplicates Yes, access O(1) by index, search O(n) — use for fixed data, heterogeneous records, safer data
Comparison row — Set: mutable Yes, ordered No, duplicates No, access N/A, search O(1) avg — use for uniqueness, membership testing, set operations
Comparison row — Dict: mutable Yes, ordered Yes* (insertion order since 3.7+), duplicate keys No, access O(1) avg by key, search O(1) avg by key — use for key-value mapping and fast lookup by key
Comparison row — deque: mutable Yes, ordered Yes, duplicates Yes, access O(1) from both ends, search O(n) — use for frequent insertions/deletions at both ends (queue, sliding window)

Decision flowchart: Unique items only? → Yes: use Set; No → Need key-value lookup? → Yes: use Dict; No → Need frequent add/remove at both ends? → Yes: use deque; No → Is data fixed/constant? → Yes: use Tuple; No → use List
Scenario: store items of a shopping cart → List (order matters, duplicates allowed); store coordinates (x,y) of a point → Tuple (fixed pair of values)
Scenario: remove duplicates from a list → Set; check if an email already exists in the system → Set (fast membership check)
Scenario: store user info (id, name, email) → Dict (lookup by id or email); implement a task queue (FIFO) → deque
Scenario: implement undo/redo in an editor → List used as a stack (LIFO); count frequency of words in a file → Dict (word → count)
Mistake: using a list for membership testing → O(n); use a set → O(1) avg
Mistake: using a list as a dict key → error; use a tuple or string instead
Mistake: using a dict when you only need unique values → use a set; using a list with `pop(0)` for a queue → O(n), use deque; using a tuple when modifications are needed → use a list
Tip: think in terms of the operations you need to perform and pick the structure that makes those operations fast
Remember: the right choice of data structure can reduce time complexity from O(n) to O(1) in many cases

At a glance cards — List: dynamic array, ordered, duplicates OK, best for general purpose; Tuple: immutable list, ordered, duplicates OK, best for fixed data; Set: hash table, unordered, unique items, best for membership tests; Dict: hash table, insertion ordered, unique keys, best for key-value mapping; deque: doubly linked list, ordered, duplicates OK, best for queue/sliding window
Key takeaway: there is no one-size-fits-all — understand the trade-offs

chapters.title: Summary & Best Practices
points: Summary: lists are ordered, mutable and allow duplicates; tuples are ordered, immutable and allow duplicates
Summary: sets are unordered, mutable and store unique items; dictionaries are ordered, mutable and store key-value pairs with unique keys
Summary: stacks (LIFO) and queues (FIFO) are special use cases implemented using lists or `collections.deque` for better performance; choosing the right structure improves time and space efficiency
When to use what — List: ordered collection, frequent changes, duplicates allowed; Tuple: fixed data, heterogeneous records, or as a dict key
When to use what — Set: unique items, membership check, mathematical operations; Dict: key-value mapping, fast lookup by key; deque: fast appends/pops from both ends (queues, sliding window)
Cheatsheet — Access (by index/key): List O(1), Tuple O(1), Set –, Dict O(1) avg, deque O(1)
Cheatsheet — Search (by value): List O(n), Tuple O(n), Set O(1) avg, Dict O(1) avg, deque O(n)
Cheatsheet — Insert: List O(1) end / O(n) other, Tuple –, Set O(1) avg, Dict O(1) avg, deque O(1); Delete: same pattern as insert
Cheatsheet — Membership test: List O(n), Tuple O(n), Set O(1) avg, Dict O(1) avg, deque O(n); note 'avg' means average case — worst case for set/dict can degrade to O(n) due to collisions
Code snippet — list comprehension: `squares = [x*x for x in range(1,6)]` → [1,4,9,16,25]
Code snippet — dict comprehension: `d = {x: x*x for x in range(1,4)}` → {1:1, 2:4, 3:9}; set comprehension: `s = {x%2 for x in range(10)}` → {0,1}
Code snippet — deque: `from collections import deque`; `dq=deque([1,2,3])`; `dq.appendleft(0)` → [0,1,2,3]; `dq.pop()` → 3
Pattern — Two Sum using dict: `seen={}` then `for i,x in enumerate(nums): if target-x in seen: return [seen[target-x], i]; seen[x]=i`
Pattern — sliding window using deque over a value strip; frequency count using dict: `freq={}` then `for ch in s: freq[ch]=freq.get(ch,0)+1`

Best practices: prefer dict for lookups over list; use set for membership tests and removing duplicates; use deque for queues and sliding windows; avoid modifying a list while iterating over it; understand time complexity before choosing; write clean, readable, pythonic code

Memory usage (rough): List more memory (stores references + over-allocation); Tuple less memory (fixed size, compact); Set more memory (hash table overhead); Dict more memory (key + value + hash table); deque moderate memory (optimized for ends)
Final thought: every problem has many solutions, but not every solution is efficient — mastering data structures helps you write better, faster and scalable code
Interview tip: while answering, first clarify requirements before picking a structure
